record.paper_title: Twenty Open Questions in Supersymmetric Particle Physics
record.original_question: The MSSM contains many physical CP-violating phases beyond the single Standard Model phase, and these phases can contribute to neutron electric dipole moments and kaon CP violation without the strong suppressions present in the Standard Model. Why are large supersymmetric CP-violating effects not ubiquitous in present experiments, and are the phases small, the relevant superpartners heavy, the scalar masses degenerate or decoupled, or the supersymmetry-breaking mechanism specially structured?

evidence.quote: Question #3 Why isn’t CP violation ubiquitous?
In the MSSM there are 43 physical CP-violating phases above and beyond that of the SM.
Clearly, if the phases φA,B take values of O(1), then the sparticles must be heavier than 1 TeV; or for sparticles around 100 GeV, the phases must be less than about 10−2.
The CP problem is solved in ways that are similar to those that solve the flavor problem.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), a supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model of particle physics in which every Standard Model fermion is paired with a bosonic superpartner (and vice versa), and which contains two Higgs doublets together with their fermionic superpartners. After eliminating phases removable by field redefinitions, the MSSM Lagrangian contains 43 physical CP-violating phases in addition to the single Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa phase of the Standard Model. Among these are the phases φ_μ of the supersymmetric Higgs mass parameter μ and φ_A of the trilinear soft-breaking couplings A, as well as phases in the gaugino masses and the squark/slepton mass matrices. Generic O(1) values of such phases, with superpartner masses around the electroweak scale (∼100 GeV), lead to contributions to the electric dipole moment of the neutron and to CP-violating observables in the neutral kaon system (such as ε_K and ε'/ε) that exceed current experimental bounds by several orders of magnitude, without the GIM-type suppression operative in the Standard Model. Phenomenological viability therefore requires one of: (i) the new CP-violating phases are universally small (e.g. |φ_{A,B}| ≲ 10^{-2}); (ii) the relevant superpartners are heavy (squarks and sleptons of the first two generations above ∼1 TeV); (iii) the soft scalar mass matrices are nearly degenerate or aligned so as to suppress flavor-changing and CP-violating effects; or (iv) the underlying mechanism of supersymmetry breaking has a special structure (such as gauge mediation, anomaly mediation, or specific flavor symmetries) that automatically produces small or aligned phases.

Problem. Determine, within the framework of the MSSM (or any well-motivated extension), the mechanism that naturally reconciles the presence of generic supersymmetric CP-violating phases with the stringent experimental upper bounds on the neutron and electron electric dipole moments and on CP violation in the kaon and B-meson systems. Specifically, identify which combination of the alternatives above (small phases, heavy superpartners, scalar degeneracy/decoupling, or structured supersymmetry breaking) is realized in nature, and construct an explicit, predictive model of supersymmetry breaking and mediation in which the suppression of supersymmetric CP-violating effects follows from symmetry or dynamics rather than fine tuning.
artifact.status_search_result: The supersymmetric CP problem remains an open question in particle physics. As of 2026, despite many proposed solutions (heavy first/second-generation sfermions, alignment, gauge/anomaly mediation, approximate CP symmetries), no superpartners have been discovered at the LHC, and tightening EDM bounds (notably ACME and neutron EDM experiments) continue to constrain supersymmetric phases without selecting a definitive mechanism. Recent reviews continue to list the SUSY CP problem as unresolved.

status_evidence.snippet: The SUSY CP problem persists: generic O(1) phases yield EDMs orders of magnitude above bounds, requiring suppression mechanisms.
status_evidence.claim: The SUSY CP problem is recognized as an outstanding issue requiring either small phases, heavy sfermions, or special structure.

status_evidence.title: ACME II electron EDM bound
status_evidence.snippet: Improved limit |d_e|<1.1e-29 e cm further constrains BSM CP-violating phases.
status_evidence.claim: Experimental EDM bounds continue to tighten, sustaining the SUSY CP problem without resolving it.
